feed.title: Re: Safer sighashes and more granular SIGHASH_NOINPUT

entry.title: Re: Safer sighashes and more granular SIGHASH_NOINPUT
entry.summary:
The scenario involving miner policies for handling malleated transactions presents a complex landscape. Miners often encounter transactions that have undergone some form of malleability, meaning their signatures or scripts have been modified in such a way that the transaction ID changes, but the underlying transaction remains valid and spendable. While miners would prefer to include non-malleated variants, which are less problematic and typically more desirable, they might not have access to these alternatives immediately. Given this uncertainty, it is economically rational for miners to accept malleated transactions into their mempools if those transactions offer competitive fee rates. This approach maximizes potential profit since rejecting such transactions outright could diminish their earnings.
However, accepting malleated transactions introduces risks, particularly the possibility of Denial of Service (DoS) attacks. Attackers could exploit the willingness of miners to accept these transactions by flooding the network with malleated versions, leading to resource exhaustion or confusion over which variant to confirm. To counteract this, miners may consider implementing Replace-by-Fee (RBF) policies that only allow replacement transactions if there is a substantial increase in the fee rate. Alternatively, some suggest rejecting malleated transactions altogether to avoid exposure to these vulnerabilities, though this approach may also carry economic downsides.
A review of weight-malleable opcodes reveals that the list is shorter than expected, indicating that the scope of potential malleability exploits may be limited in practice. Strengthening consensus rules through measures like enforcing MINIMAL_IF and minimal CScriptNum requirements could prove effective. By integrating these updates into future versions of Script, it becomes feasible to almost entirely eliminate weight malleability, thereby reducing the attack surface and improving transaction reliability across the network.
